questions.q: What is the exact symbol used to start a single-line comment in Python, and what happens to the text following that symbol on the same line during program execution?
questions.a: The symbol is `#` (hash). Everything from `#` to the end of that physical line is ignored by the Python interpreter and produces no output or error. A wrong answer (e.g., `//` or `/*`) reveals confusion with C++/Java syntax; a wrong answer about execution (e.g., "it prints as text") reveals the student thinks comments are string literals.

questions.q:
A student writes the following three lines in a Python script and runs it. Explain what will happen and why:
```
questions.a: The program will output `Hello` only. The first line is a full-line comment (ignored). The second line executes `print("Hello")`; the part after `#` is an inline comment (ignored). The third line is a multi-line comment using triple single quotes — it is a string literal not assigned to any variable, so it is evaluated and discarded (no output). A wrong answer (e.g., "syntax error on line 3" or "prints the triple-quoted text") reveals the misconception that triple-quoted strings are a special comment syntax rather than unused string expressions.

questions.q: Write a Python code snippet (3-4 lines) that calculates the area of a rectangular plot (length=12.5 m, breadth=8.3 m) and uses: (a) a single-line comment to state the formula, (b) a multi-line comment to describe the program's purpose and input units, and (c) an inline comment on the calculation line.
questions.a:
```python
''' 
Program: Calculate area of rectangular plot
Inputs: length and breadth in metres
Output: area in square metres
'''
length = 12.5  # metres
breadth = 8.3  # metres
area = length * breadth  # Formula: Area = length × breadth
print("Area =", area, "sq m")
```
A wrong answer (missing triple quotes, using `#` for multi-line, or putting inline comment before code) reveals inability to apply both comment styles contextually.

questions.q:
Compare the following two multi-line comment blocks. Which one is technically a string literal that exists at runtime (occupies memory), and why does this distinction matter in a long-running program like a server?
```python
questions.a: Block A is a string literal (triple-quoted) — it is created in memory at runtime and immediately discarded because it is not assigned. Block B uses only `#` comments, which are stripped by the lexer and never exist at runtime. In a long-running server, repeated execution of Block A (e.g., inside a loop) creates unnecessary memory churn (garbage collection pressure), while Block B has zero runtime cost. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are same" or "Block B uses more memory") reveals lack of understanding of Python's execution model (lexing vs. evaluation).

questions.q: A team member argues: "We should comment every single line of code so that anyone can understand it." Evaluate this statement. Is it a good practice? Justify your answer with two specific reasons related to code maintenance and readability.
questions.a: No, it is not good practice. (1) **Redundancy**: Comments that merely restate the code (e.g., `x = x + 1  # increment x by 1`) add noise and violate the DRY principle — when code changes, comments often become outdated, creating misinformation. (2) **Readability**: Excessive comments obscure the actual logic; clean, well-named variables and functions (self-documenting code) are superior. Comments should explain *why* (intent, constraints, business rules), not *what*. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "yes, more comments are always better") reveals a novice mindset that equates quantity of comments with quality of documentation.
